On the balcony of their fourth-floor flat in Chennai, Ramesh spun in circles with a steel plate on his head, stamping his feet. "Rain, rain, come on!" The colony cricket match had been called off because of the heat, and he was bored.
Ten minutes later the sky went grey and fat drops hit the railing.
"I DID IT!" Ramesh shouted. "Yamini akka, my dance made it rain!"
Yamini, pulling clothes off the line in a hurry, laughed. "The weather report said rain this evening. It was on the news at lunch."
"But it came right after my dance."
"And if you hadn't danced?"
Ramesh thought about it, dripping. "Then... maybe it would still come?" He did one more spin, just in case.

qa.q: What did Ramesh have on his head while dancing?
qa.a: A steel plate.

qa.q: Why is Ramesh so sure his dance brought the rain?
qa.a: The rain came right after he danced, so it felt like his dance had worked, and he loved the idea of making it happen. 😊

qa.q: Which question from Yamini akka helped, and why?
qa.a: "And if you hadn't danced?" made Ramesh picture the rain coming anyway, since it had already been forecast.

qa.q: How does Yamini akka see Ramesh's rain dance?
qa.a: She finds it funny and knows the rain was on the lunchtime news, but she lets him work it out instead of scolding.

grounding: It shows a boy believing his dance caused the rain simply because the rain came after it.

"I'm never eating ice cream again," Kamal croaked from under the blanket. "Never."
Arohi didi sat on the edge of his bed with a glass of warm water. "Why?"
"I had one kulfi at Raju's party on Sunday, and now I have fever. It's the kulfi."
"Half your class has fever this week. Your class teacher sent a note."
"But I got it right after the kulfi."
"You got it two days after. And what else happened in two days?"
Kamal thought. "Joseph coughed on me in the van."
"Hmm."
"So maybe it's Joseph's cough, not the kulfi?"
"Maybe. Mummy's taking you to the doctor this evening anyway. Ask the doctor."
"Can I ask about kulfi?"
"Ask everything."

qa.q: What did Kamal eat at Raju's party?
qa.a: One kulfi.

qa.q: Why does Kamal blame the kulfi for his fever?
qa.a: Kamal feels miserable and blames the kulfi because the fever came after it, so in his mind one led to the other, and it's the unusual thing he remembers doing.

qa.q: How did Arohi didi help Kamal think again?
qa.a: She pointed out that half his class had fever and asked what else happened in two days, which let him remember Joseph's cough himself.

qa.q: How might Arohi didi feel watching her little brother swear off ice cream?
qa.a: She probably finds it a little funny but also feels for him being unwell, which is why she sits with him and brings warm water.

grounding: It shows a boy blaming one kulfi for his fever because the fever came afterwards.

passage: When I was eight, I had a goldfish called Biscuit. My name is Francis, and Mum still calls me her goldfish boy because of what happened. One night I forgot to say goodnight to Biscuit, and the next morning he was floating sideways and not eating. I was sure it was my fault. That night I said goodnight three times, very loudly. The next day he was swimming again! I told everyone at school that saying goodnight had cured him. My sister Ankita just rolled her eyes. What I didn't mention was that she had cleaned his whole tank that same evening, because the water was dirty. Now I'm ten and I think it was the clean water. Back then, the goodnight felt like magic, because it came right before he got better.

qa.q: What had Ankita done that same evening?
qa.a: She had cleaned his whole tank, because the water was dirty.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel it was his fault when Biscuit got sick?
qa.a: Francis felt guilty because he had forgotten to say goodnight the night before, and since the sickness came right after, it seemed to be caused by it.

qa.q: What could Francis ask himself next time something seems to work like magic?
qa.a: What else happened at the same time, like the clean water, and would it have got better anyway?

qa.q: How might Ankita feel hearing Francis tell everyone that goodnight cured Biscuit?
qa.a: She might feel a bit unnoticed, since she did the real work of cleaning the tank, and also amused at the story.

grounding: It shows a boy believing his goodnight cured his goldfish because the recovery came right after it.

Class 3 garden note, Monday (Ms Kulkarni)
Last Wednesday each child planted two bean seeds in a cup. On Thursday, Ujjwal, 8, whistled a tune to his cup before lunch. On Saturday both his seeds sprouted.
Today he told the class, "I whistled to them and they came out. Whistling makes beans grow." Two children started whistling at their cups at once.
Kishore pointed out that his own beans had sprouted too, and he had never whistled. Ujjwal said, "Maybe you hummed and forgot."
I didn't tell him he was wrong. I asked the class to set up two new cups each: whistle to one, keep the other quiet, and draw both every morning.
Next: check the drawings on Friday and let Ujjwal say what he sees first.

qa.q: When did Ujjwal's seeds sprout?
qa.a: On Saturday both his seeds sprouted.

qa.q: Why does it feel certain to Ujjwal that whistling made the beans grow?
qa.a: He whistled first and the sprouts came after, so the order of events makes it feel like one caused the other, and even Kishore's beans don't shake that feeling.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms Kulkarni was a good turning point, and why?
qa.a: Setting up two cups each, one with whistling and one without, lets Ujjwal see for himself whether the whistling changes anything, instead of being told he is wrong.

qa.q: What would change if Ms Kulkarni had just laughed at Ujjwal's idea?
qa.a: Ujjwal might feel embarrassed and stop sharing ideas, and he would miss the chance to test it himself with the two cups.

grounding: It shows a child deciding that whistling to his seeds made them sprout just because the sprouting came after the whistling.

Thursday
I have fever today. Amma put a wet cloth on my head and said I'm still her brave boy.
I KNOW why I got it. Yesterday after football I drank cold water straight from the tap, a big glass, very fast. And today, fever. So cold water gives fever. I'm never drinking cold water again, not even in summer.
I told Amma. She said Varun has fever too, and half my class is absent, and Varun only drinks warm water because his Nani makes him.
That's different. Varun probably drank something cold and didn't tell.
Amma is taking me to the doctor tomorrow if it keeps going. I'm going to tell the doctor about the tap.
Pema

qa.a: Cold water straight from the tap, a big glass, very fast.

qa.q: Why is Pema so sure the cold water caused the fever?
qa.a: The fever came the day after the cold water, so it feels as if one made the other happen, and Pema explains away Varun's fever to keep the idea.

qa.a: Pema could ask why Varun and half the class got fever too when they didn't all drink cold water, which points to something else going around.

qa.q: What might Amma be thinking when she mentions Varun and the absent classmates?
qa.a: Amma seems to think the fever is going around the class, and gently wants Pema to see that the cold water is not the likely reason.

grounding: It shows a child believing his fever came from drinking cold water once, because the fever followed it.
